title: ArrayDeque vs LinkedList vs Stack — when to use each
shortTitle: ArrayDeque vs LinkedList vs Stack — when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: `ArrayDeque` is a resizable circular array implementing `Deque` — double-ended queue with O(1) amortized add/remove at BOTH ends. It's **faster than LinkedList** as a queue (cache locality) and **faster than Stack** as a stack (no synchronization overhead). **Use ArrayDeque** for: queue (FIFO), stack (LIFO), and deque (both ends). **Don't use LinkedList** as a Deque — ArrayDeque beats it in virtually every benchmark due to contiguous memory. **Don't use Stack** class — it extends Vector (legacy synchronized), allows random access by index (violates stack abstraction), and is slower.
s1_definition.analogy: **ArrayDeque** = modern bank counter with two windows (front + back), fast service, no unnecessary paperwork. **LinkedList as Deque** = chain of sticky notes — works but scattered across the building, slower to process. **Stack (legacy)** = old counter with a heavy lock on the door — even one customer waits for the lock to open. ArrayDeque: best of all worlds.
s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayDeque = fastest Deque/Stack/Queue. Beats LinkedList (cache locality). Beats Stack (no sync overhead). Default choice for queue, stack, and deque.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ArrayDeque` is a resizable circular array implementing `Deque` — double-ended queue with O(1) amortized add/remove at BOTH ends. It's **faster than LinkedList** as a queue (cache locality) and **faster than Stack** as a stack (no synchronization overhead). **Use ArrayDeque** for: queue (FIFO), stack (LIFO), and deque (both ends). **Don't use LinkedList** as a Deque — ArrayDeque beats it in virtually every benchmark due to contiguous memory. **Don't use Stack** class — it extends Vector (legacy synchronized), allows random access by index (violates stack abstraction), and is slower.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **ArrayDeque** = modern bank counter with two windows (front + back), fast service, no unnecessary paperwork. **LinkedList as Deque** = chain of sticky notes — works but scattered across the building, slower to process. **Stack (legacy)** = old counter with a heavy lock on the door — even one customer waits for the lock to open. ArrayDeque: best of all worlds.

**One line to remember:** ArrayDeque = fastest Deque/Stack/Queue. Beats LinkedList (cache locality). Beats Stack (no sync overhead). Default choice for queue, stack, and deque.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The undo/redo feature used `Stack` class** (extends Vector). Performance profiling showed 20% overhead from synchronized methods — even though only one thread used the undo stack. Also, developers accidentally used `stack.get(3)` (random access) — violating LIFO principle. Fix: replaced `Stack` with `ArrayDeque` — no sync overhead, no random access API (push/pop/peek only), 3x faster.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a series of transaction events pushed and popped using three different structures.

**Step 1.** An `ArrayDeque` pushes each event onto a resizable circular array, giving fast O(1) add and remove at both ends with no node overhead.

**Step 2.** A `LinkedList` does the same but allocates a node object per event, adding memory overhead and poorer cache locality.

**Step 3.** The legacy `Stack` works too but is synchronized and slower, so for Rajesh's undo history the modern `ArrayDeque` is the recommended LIFO choice.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ArrayDeque CIRCULAR ARRAY ═══

  Internal array: [_][_][C][D][E][_][_][_]
                        ↑       ↑
                       head    tail
  addFirst("B"): head moves LEFT  → [_][B][C][D][E][_][_][_]
  addLast("F"):  tail moves RIGHT → [_][B][C][D][E][F][_][_]
  Wraps around when reaching array boundary!

  ═══ DECISION: which to use? ═══

  Need LIFO (stack)?     → ArrayDeque.push/pop    (NOT Stack class!)
  Need FIFO (queue)?     → ArrayDeque.offer/poll   (NOT LinkedList!)
  Need both ends (deque)?→ ArrayDeque              (fastest!)
  Need null elements?    → LinkedList              (ArrayDeque rejects null)
  Need List + Deque?     → LinkedList              (implements both)
  Default?               → ArrayDeque              (always!)
```

```
  │ ArrayDeque<Transaction>       │  circular array
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
   Queue mode:  offerLast / pollFirst  (FIFO pipeline)

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayDeque is the best general-purpose Deque/Stack/Queue implementation. It's backed by a resizable circular array — O(1) amortized add/remove at both ends, excellent cache locality (contiguous memory), and no synchronization overhead. It beats LinkedList as a Deque (2-3x faster in benchmarks due to cache locality, 5x less memory per element). It beats Stack class as a stack (no synchronized overhead, no inappropriate random access API).

ArrayDeque limitations: cannot store null elements (null is used as internal empty marker), doesn't implement `List` (no `get(index)`), and grows by doubling (2x) which can waste memory. Use LinkedList only when you need both List and Deque interfaces on the same object, or when you need null elements. The Java docs explicitly state: "This class is likely to be faster than Stack when used as a stack, and faster than LinkedList when used as a queue." In banking: transaction processing queue → ArrayDeque. Undo/redo → ArrayDeque. Never Stack class, rarely LinkedList.
